implementation_notes: Go has the tightest measure-first loop of any mainstream language, because the tooling is built in and free: pprof (cpu, heap, block, mutex profiles), the block and mutex profiles being unusual and valuable, and `go test -bench` with -benchmem for allocations. The micro-optimisations that pay at a measured Go hotspot are preallocating slices and maps (the escape and allocation profiles show where), avoiding interface boxing in a hot path, reducing pointer chasing by storing values in a slice of structs, and using the right container. Go's compiler does little itself (no aggressive inlining of complex functions, no vectorisation), so more of the wins are in the source than in a JIT-heavy language - but the discipline is identical. The Go-specific trap is the loop-variable capture and the deferred call in a hot loop (a defer in a per-iteration function is a real cost), and pprof's sampling can mislead on a very short run.
idiom_name: pprof (cpu/heap/block/mutex) plus go test -bench -benchmem, applied at the measured hotspot; preallocation is the usual win
code_sketch:
# 1. PROFILE (built in, free):
#   go test -bench=. -cpuprofile=cpu.out ./...
#   go tool pprof -top cpu.out
#   go test -bench=. -benchmem -memprofile=mem.out ./...
#   go tool pprof -top -alloc_space mem.out
#   (block and mutex profiles show blocking - unique to Go and very useful)

# 3. ONE CHANGE at the measured hotspot. The usual Go wins:
func Sum(points []Point) float64 {   // []Point is contiguous; []*Point chases
    var s float64
    for _, p := range points { s += p.X + p.Y }   // the profile showed the chase
    return s
}

func Build(n int) []Item {
    out := make([]Item, 0, n)      // preallocate: the allocation profile showed it
    for i := 0; i < n; i++ { out = append(out, Item{i}) }
    return out
}

# 4. VERIFY: go test -bench=. -benchmem -count=10 (the -count shows the variance)
# 5. GUARD: keep the benchmark in CI.
# TRAP: pprof SAMPLES - a very short run may not sample the hotspot at all.
# TRAP: a defer in a per-iteration hot function is a real cost Go does not remove.
pitfalls: pprof samples: a run too short may not sample the hotspot at all, so 'no hotspot found' means 'not sampled', not 'not hot'.
The allocation profile is usually more actionable than the CPU profile in Go, because most Go hot paths are allocation-bound rather than compute-bound.
A defer inside a hot per-iteration function is a real cost Go does not optimise away - check -benchmem.
An interface value or a []*T slice boxes or chases where a concrete type or a []T would not; the CPU profile shows it as cache misses rather than as an obvious 'call'.
Benchmarking a slice that is still growing: preallocate, or the benchmark measures the reallocation rather than the work.
